concepts.name: Origins and Precursors of the Subsidiary Alliance System
key_dimensions: Role of Duplex (French) in originating the concept of using Indian rulers to fund European troops
Warren Hastings' and Cornwallis's earlier subsidiary-type arrangements vs. Wellesley's formalized version
Distinction between Ring-fence policy (Cornwallis) and Subsidiary Alliance (Wellesley) — purpose and scope
How the system evolved from ad hoc military agreements to a structured political instrument

concepts.name: Core Terms and Mechanics of the Subsidiary Alliance Treaty
key_dimensions: The Indian ruler surrenders control of foreign policy and external relations to the British
Obligation to maintain a British Resident at the court and expel other European nationals
Payment of subsidy (cash or territorial cession) in exchange for British military protection
Prohibition on entering alliances or making war without British consent — the 'sovereignty trap'

concepts.name: Lord Wellesley's Strategic Motivation Behind the System
key_dimensions: Eliminating French influence in India during the Napoleonic Wars period (post-1798 context)
Generating revenue and territorial gains for the Company without direct annexation
Converting Indian princes from potential enemies into dependent allies under British paramountcy
Wellesley's vision of British Empire vs. the Court of Directors' commercial/non-interventionist preference

concepts.name: Hyderabad — First State to Accept Subsidiary Alliance (1798 & 1800)
key_dimensions: First treaty of 1798 and its revised/strengthened version in 1800 — key differences
Dissolution of Hyderabad's French-trained contingent as a direct outcome
Territorial concession of Berar districts in lieu of cash subsidy — template for future treaties
UPSC trap: Hyderabad accepted before Mysore — chronological sequencing questions

concepts.name: Mysore and the Subsidiary Alliance (1799)
key_dimensions: Fourth Anglo-Mysore War (1799) and fall of Tipu Sultan as the precondition
Restoration of Wadiyar dynasty — Mysore not annexed but placed under subsidiary alliance
Mysore as an example of 'indirect rule' through subsidiary alliance post-conquest
Contrast with Tipu Sultan's refusal — why refusal led to war while acceptance preserved dynasties

concepts.name: The Nizam of Hyderabad vs. Tipu Sultan — Case Study in Acceptance vs. Rejection
key_dimensions: Why Nizam accepted (weak, threatened by Marathas and Mysore) vs. why Tipu rejected (strong, ideological resistance)
Outcome divergence: Nizam survived as a subsidiary; Tipu was destroyed
Demonstrates the coercive logic of the system — 'accept and survive or resist and perish'
UPSC trap: Testing whether candidates conflate Nizam's alliance with Tipu's defeat

concepts.name: Tanjore, Surat, and Carnatic — Subsidiary Alliance Leading to Outright Annexation
key_dimensions: Cases where subsidiary arrangement was a stepping stone to full annexation
Nawab of Carnatic's inability to pay subsidy leading to British takeover of administration
Distinction between states that retained nominal sovereignty vs. those absorbed entirely
UPSC trap: Subsidiary alliance is not always a permanent arrangement — it could lead to annexation

concepts.name: Marathas and the Subsidiary Alliance — Treaty of Bassein (1802)
key_dimensions: Peshwa Baji Rao II accepting Subsidiary Alliance after defeat at Poona by Holkar
Treaty of Bassein (December 31, 1802) — terms and significance
Reaction of Sindhia and Bhonsle — Second Anglo-Maratha War as direct consequence
UPSC trap: Treaty of Bassein signed by Peshwa, not all Maratha chiefs — partial acceptance leading to war

concepts.name: Awadh (Oudh) and the Subsidiary Alliance (1801)
key_dimensions: Forced nature of the 1801 treaty — Wellesley's coercive diplomacy with Nawab Saadat Ali Khan
Cession of Rohilkhand, Gorakhpur, and Doab — massive territorial loss
Awadh retained as a 'buffer state' but completely dependent — classic 'velvet annexation'
Later annexation in 1856 by Dalhousie — subsidiary alliance as a long-term prelude to annexation

concepts.name: The Subsidiary Alliance as an Instrument of Paramountcy
key_dimensions: How it established British 'paramountcy' (supreme authority) over Indian princes without formal annexation
Difference between paramountcy and sovereignty — Indian rulers lost external sovereignty but retained internal
Continuity with later policies: how paramountcy doctrine persisted until 1947
UPSC conceptual trap: Paramountcy ≠ sovereignty; Indian states were 'allies' not 'subjects' in theory

concepts.name: Financial Dimensions — Subsidy Payment and Territorial Cession Clause
key_dimensions: Cash subsidy vs. territorial cession — which states paid cash, which ceded territory
How territorial cessions enriched Company's revenue base (e.g., Tanjore, Surat, Carnatic)
Criticism: subsidy demands were deliberately set beyond the capacity of Indian rulers to pay
Connection between financial inability to pay subsidy and eventual British takeover of administration

concepts.name: The British Resident — Role, Powers, and Political Significance
key_dimensions: The Resident as de facto ruler — interference in internal administration despite treaty terms
Residents as intelligence gatherers and political agents advancing British interests
Contrast between formal treaty terms (non-interference in internal affairs) and actual practice
UPSC trap: Treaty said no interference in internal matters, but Residents routinely intervened

concepts.name: Impact on Indian Military Power and State Finances
key_dimensions: Disbanding of Indian rulers' independent armies — destruction of military capacity
Maintenance of British subsidiary force was expensive, draining state treasuries
Impoverishment of Indian states leading to neglect of administration and public welfare
Long-term effect: weakened Indian states could not resist further British encroachment

concepts.name: Criticism by British Authorities — Court of Directors vs. Wellesley
key_dimensions: Court of Directors opposed the system as too expensive and aggressive — conflict with Wellesley
Wellesley recalled in 1805 partly due to the aggressive expansion policy
Arguments against: financial overextension, unnecessary wars triggered by the system (Maratha Wars)
UPSC trap: Wellesley was recalled — his policy was controversial even within British establishment

concepts.name: Comparison with Doctrine of Lapse (Dalhousie) — Continuity in British Expansion
key_dimensions: Subsidiary Alliance: indirect control through dependence; Doctrine of Lapse: direct annexation through succession manipulation
Both targeted Indian princely states but through different mechanisms
Chronological distinction: Wellesley (1798–1805) vs. Dalhousie (1848–1856)
UPSC overlap trap: Students confuse which states were taken under which policy — need precise mapping

concepts.name: Subsidiary Alliance vs. Ring-Fence Policy — Conceptual Distinction
key_dimensions: Ring-fence (Cornwallis/Hastings): creating a buffer zone to protect British territory — defensive in nature
Subsidiary Alliance (Wellesley): offensive, expansionist — aimed at establishing control over all Indian powers
Ring-fence kept Indian states outside British sphere; Subsidiary Alliance pulled them into dependency
UPSC trap: Both involve military arrangements with Indian states but have opposite strategic orientations

concepts.name: States That Refused the Subsidiary Alliance and Consequences
key_dimensions: Tipu Sultan's refusal — led to Fourth Anglo-Mysore War and his death (1799)
Ranjit Singh (Punjab) successfully avoided subsidiary alliance throughout his reign — exception to note
Nepal — resisted and fought Anglo-Nepal War (1814–16) but was not brought under subsidiary alliance
UPSC trap: Not every state that resisted was conquered — Ranjit Singh's Punjab is a critical exception

concepts.name: Long-Term Political Consequence — Princes' Political Isolation
key_dimensions: Indian rulers could not form coalitions against the British — each was isolated in a bilateral relationship
The system prevented any pan-Indian political solidarity among princes
Contributed to the failure of 1857 uprising — many subsidiary-alliance states did not join or actively supported British
UPSC analytical question: How did Subsidiary Alliance contribute to the success of British paramountcy by 1857?

concepts.name: Subsidiary Alliance and the Doctrine of Paramountcy — Legal and Constitutional Implications
key_dimensions: How subsidiary treaties formed the legal basis for British claims of paramountcy
Butler Committee (1927) and its examination of paramountcy in the context of these treaties
Paramountcy lapsing in 1947 — Indian states technically became independent, creating the integration challenge
UPSC linkage: Subsidiary Alliance → Paramountcy → Lapse of Paramountcy → Sardar Patel's integration challenge

concepts.name: Wellesley's Subsidiary Alliance as a Tool of 'Informal Empire'
key_dimensions: Concept of 'informal empire': control without formal annexation — Wellesley as its pioneer in India
Comparison with British informal empire in China, Ottoman Empire, Latin America (broader UPSC GS context)
How the system allowed Britain to dominate India's political landscape while minimizing administrative burden
Historiographical debate: Was Wellesley's system a stroke of genius or reckless imperialism? — Essay/opinion question angle
